title: Political Parties and Party Systems
outline: Meaning and features of a political party

modules.title: Nature and Functions of Political Parties
modules.html:
1. Definition and Features

A political party is an organised group of people sharing broadly similar political beliefs, whose principal aim is to capture and control the machinery of government through constitutional means, usually elections.

Features: organised structure from ward to national level; a constitution and manifesto; identifiable symbol, name and motto; voluntary membership; a broad programme covering national issues; commitment to winning power lawfully; sources of funds; discipline over members.

2. Functions

  1. Contesting elections and forming government.
  2. Recruiting and grooming political leaders.
  3. Aggregating and articulating interests into coherent programmes.
  4. Political education and socialisation of the electorate.
  5. Organising opposition and criticising government (the 'shadow' role).
  6. Serving as a link between government and the people.
  7. Promoting national integration where parties are nationwide.
  8. Ensuring accountability through internal and inter-party competition.

3. Party versus Pressure Group

CriterionPolitical partyPressure group
AimCapture governmentInfluence government
Scope of interestBroad, nationalNarrow, sectional
ElectionsSponsors candidatesDoes not normally contest
ResponsibilityAccountable if it forms governmentBears no governmental responsibility

examples.q: Why is a trade union not a political party even when it endorses a candidate?
examples.a: Its primary purpose is to protect the sectional interest of its members — wages and conditions — not to capture government. It does not present a comprehensive national programme, does not field candidates under its own name, and bears no responsibility for governing. Endorsement is a pressure tactic, not party competition. Where a union does form a party (as with the Labour Party's origins), the new body becomes a party in its own right.

examples.q: Explain the function of a shadow cabinet.
examples.a: In parliamentary systems the main opposition party appoints spokesmen mirroring each government minister. They scrutinise the corresponding ministry, offer alternative policies and prepare to take office if their party wins. This institutionalises criticism, sharpens accountability, and trains future ministers.

modules.title: Party Systems and Party Organisation
modules.html:
1. Types of Party System

SystemDescriptionMeritsDemeritsExample
One-partyOnly one legal partyNational unity, avoids ethnic party rivalry, cheapDictatorship, no alternative, apathy, no accountabilityGhana under Nkrumah; Tanzania under Nyerere
Two-partyTwo dominant parties alternate in powerClear choice, stable majority government, effective oppositionLimits choice, may exclude minorities, encourages polarisationUSA, UK; Nigeria 1989–1993 (SDP and NRC)
Multi-partySeveral parties competeWide choice, reflects diversity, protects minoritiesCoalition instability, expensive, weak governmentsNigeria's Fourth Republic, India, Italy

2. Organisation

Nigerian parties are structured from the ward through the local government and state to the national level, with organs including the National Convention (supreme organ), National Executive Committee, National Working Committee, and caucuses. Candidates emerge through primaries, which may be direct (all members vote), indirect (delegates vote) or by consensus.

3. Party Finance and Discipline

  • Sources: membership dues, nomination fees, levies on office holders, donations, fundraising, and (formerly) government grants.
  • Discipline: the whip system, the party constitution, suspension or expulsion, and denial of nomination. In Nigeria a legislator who defects without a division in his party may lose his seat under sections 68 and 109.

4. Parties in Nigerian History

  1. 1923 — Nigerian National Democratic Party (NNDP), Herbert Macaulay, Nigeria's first party.
  2. 1934/1936 — Nigerian Youth Movement (NYM).
  3. 1944 — NCNC (Azikiwe and Macaulay); 1951 — Action Group (Awolowo); 1951 — Northern People's Congress (Ahmadu Bello, Balewa).
  4. Second Republic (1979–1983) — NPN, UPN, NPP, GNPP, PRP, later NAP.
  5. Third Republic (1989–1993) — SDP and NRC, created by decree.
  6. Fourth Republic (1999–) — PDP, APP/ANPP, AD; later APC (2013 merger of ACN, CPC, ANPP and a faction of APGA), LP, NNPP and others.

examples.q: Why were the SDP and NRC described as government-created parties?
examples.a: After dissolving all associations in 1989, General Babangida's regime rejected the thirteen applicant associations and instead decreed two parties into existence, wrote their constitutions and manifestos, funded their secretariats and defined their ideologies as 'a little to the left' (SDP) and 'a little to the right' (NRC). They were therefore products of state engineering rather than spontaneous political association.

examples.q: Identify two dangers of ethnic-based parties, using Nigeria's First Republic.
examples.a: (i) They convert elections into ethnic censuses: NPC (North), NCNC (East) and AG (West) each dominated a region, so national contests became regional confrontations. (ii) They make coalitions fragile and encourage regional rather than national policy — contributing to the 1962 Western Region crisis, the disputed 1964 federal election and ultimately the collapse of the First Republic in 1966.

quiz.q: The primary aim of a political party is to:
quiz.solution: Parties seek to win governmental power through elections.

quiz.q: Nigeria's first political party was the:
quiz.solution: Herbert Macaulay founded the Nigerian National Democratic Party in 1923 after the Clifford Constitution introduced elections.

quiz.q: Which party was led by Obafemi Awolowo in the First Republic?
quiz.solution: Awolowo led the Action Group, formed in 1951 from the Egbe Omo Oduduwa.

quiz.q: A system with two dominant parties is a:
quiz.solution: Two major parties realistically alternate in power.

quiz.q: The SDP and NRC were created in:
quiz.solution: The Babangida regime decreed the two parties into existence in 1989.

quiz.q: A document stating a party's programme is its:
quiz.solution: The manifesto sets out promises and policies for the electorate.

quiz.q: The supreme organ of a Nigerian political party is normally the:
quiz.solution: The National Convention is the highest decision-making body of the party.

quiz.q: Party discipline in the legislature is enforced by the:
quiz.solution: The whip ensures members attend and vote along party lines.

quiz.q: A demerit of the one-party system is:
quiz.solution: With no legal opposition, citizens have no alternative and accountability weakens.

quiz.q: The APC was formed in 2013 by the merger of ACN, CPC, ANPP and a faction of:
quiz.solution: A faction of the All Progressives Grand Alliance joined the merger.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a function of political parties?
quiz.solution: Adjudication belongs to the courts, not to parties.

quiz.q: Selection of candidates within a party is done through:
quiz.solution: Party primaries, direct or indirect, nominate candidates.

quiz.q: Sections 68 and 109 of the 1999 Constitution deal with:
options: Loss of legislative seat on defection
quiz.solution: A legislator who defects without a division in his party may forfeit his seat.

quiz.q: The NCNC was founded in 1944 by Azikiwe and:
quiz.solution: Macaulay was the first president of the NCNC, with Azikiwe as secretary.

quiz.q: A multi-party system is common in societies that are:
quiz.solution: Diversity of interests produces many parties seeking representation.

quiz.q: A party's ward-level structure exists mainly to:
quiz.solution: Wards are the base units for membership registration and grassroots mobilisation.
